## Language Fundamentals

Elixir's fundamentals build on functional programming principles. Everything is an expression, pattern matching is pervasive, and immutable data is the default. Understanding these concepts is the foundation for all Elixir programming.

### Topic Notes

- [Basics](https://dart.wyattau.com/flashcards-dart-basics/), variables, atoms, tuples, lists, and maps
- [Pattern Matching](https://dart.wyattau.com/07-dart3-features/01-pattern-matching/), the match operator, pin operator, and destructuring
- [Functions](https://alevel.wyattau.com/maths/pure-mathematics/05-functions/), named functions, anonymous functions, guards, and clauses
- Modules and Attributes, module definitions, module attributes, and documentation
- [Control Flow](https://kotlin.wyattau.com/basics/control-flow/), case, cond, with, and do blocks

### Key Concepts

**Pattern matching with `=`**, The match operator destructures data. `{a, b} = {1, 2}` binds `a` to 1 and `b` to 2. Pattern matching is used in function heads, case expressions, and with chains. It is the primary way to handle different data shapes.

**Atoms** are constants whose name is their value. `:ok``:error``:not_found`atoms are lightweight and fast to compare. They are commonly used as tags, keys, and enum values.

**The `with` construct** chains operations that may fail. Each step is pattern-matched against the expected success case. If any step does not match, the non-matching value is returned. `with {:ok, data} <- fetch(url), {:ok, parsed} <- parse(data), do: {:ok, parsed}`.

---

## Functional Programming

Elixir is a functional language, functions are first-class citizens, data is immutable, and side effects are isolated. Understanding functional patterns is essential for writing idiomatic Elixir.

### Topic Notes

- [Higher-Order Functions](https://alevel.wyattau.com/maths/pure-mathematics/05-functions/), Enum.map, Enum.filter, Enum.reduce, and pipe operator
- Pipelines, the |> operator for chaining functions
- Recursion, tail call optimization and recursive patterns
- [Protocols](https://languages.wyattau.com/python/08-advanced-topics/04-protocols-dunder-methods/), polymorphism through protocol dispatch

### Key Concepts

**The pipe operator `|>`** passes the result of the left expression as the first argument to the right function. `data |> fetch() |> parse() |> save()` reads top-to-bottom, left-to-right. Pipelines make Elixir code highly readable.

**Enum module** provides powerful functions for working with collections. `Enum.map``Enum.filter``Enum.reduce``Enum.flat_map`and `Enum.group_by` cover most collection operations. The Stream module provides lazy evaluation for large datasets.

**Protocols** enable polymorphism through protocol dispatch. A protocol defines a set of functions. Types implement the protocol by providing implementations. Protocols dispatch on the type of the first argument at runtime.

---

## Processes and Concurrency

Elixir's process model is its most distinctive feature. Processes are lightweight (a few KB), isolated (no shared memory), and managed by the BEAM VM. Communication between processes uses message passing. This model eliminates data races and makes concurrent programming straightforward.

### Topic Notes

- Process Basics, spawn, send, receive, and process IDs
- GenServer, the generic server behaviour for stateful processes
- Agent and Task, simple state management and concurrent tasks
- Supervisors, monitoring, restarting, and fault tolerance
- Process Communication, message passing, selective receive, and timeouts

### Key Concepts

**Processes** are not OS threads. The BEAM VM manages thousands of processes on a single OS thread, switching between them in microseconds. Each process has its own heap and stack. Processes are cheap to create and destroy.

**GenServer** is the most commonly used OTP behaviour. It provides a synchronous request-response pattern with state. `handle_call` handles synchronous requests. `handle_cast` handles asynchronous messages. `handle_info` handles everything else.

**Supervisors** monitor processes and restart them when they crash. A supervisor defines a strategy: `:one_for_one` restarts only the failed child, `:one_for_all` restarts all children. Supervisors form a tree that provides fault tolerance.

---

## OTP

OTP (Open Telecom Platform) is a set of libraries and behaviours for building fault-tolerant applications. OTP provides GenServer, Supervisor, Application, and other behaviours that standardize common patterns.

### Topic Notes

- OTP Overview, what OTP provides and why it matters
- [Application](https://computer-science.wyattau.com/3-computer-networks/6_application-layer/), application lifecycle, configuration, and the supervision tree
- GenStateMachine, state machines with OTP
- ETS and Mnesia, in-memory storage and distributed database

### Key Concepts

**OTP applications** are the unit of deployment. An application module defines `start/2` and `stop/1`. The application starts a supervision tree that manages all processes. Configuration is stored in `config/config.exs`.

**The supervision tree** is a hierarchy of supervisors and workers. If a worker crashes, its supervisor restarts it. If a supervisor crashes, its parent supervisor restarts it. This "let it crash" philosophy makes systems self-healing.

**ETS (Erlang Term Storage)** is an in-memory key-value store. It is fast, supports concurrent access, and can be shared between processes. ETS is used for caching, configuration, and temporary data storage.

---

## Phoenix Framework

Phoenix is Elixir's web framework. It follows the MVC pattern, provides real-time capabilities with Channels, and includes tools for database access (Ecto), testing, and deployment. Phoenix is designed for concurrency and fault tolerance.

### Topic Notes

- Phoenix Basics, router, controllers, views, and templates
- Ecto and Changesets, database access, schemas, and data validation
- [Channels](https://go.wyattau.com/concurrency/channels/), WebSocket connections, real-time updates, and presence
- LiveView, server-rendered real-time UI without JavaScript
- [Testing](https://alevel.wyattau.com/computer-science/software-engineering/02-testing/), controller tests, channel tests, and LiveView tests

### Key Concepts

**Ecto** is Phoenix's database layer. Schemas map database tables to Elixir structs. Changesets validate and cast input data. Queries are composable and compile-time checked. Ecto supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, and other databases.

**Channels** provide real-time WebSocket communication. A channel handles events from connected clients. Topics group connections. Presence tracks who is online. Channels are lightweight and fault-tolerant.

**LiveView** enables real-time, server-rendered UIs without writing JavaScript. LiveViews handle events on the server and push updates to the client over WebSocket. This eliminates the client-server divide and simplifies real-time features.

---

## Testing

Elixir has excellent testing support built into the language. ExUnit is the standard test framework. It provides describe/it blocks, fixtures, async tests, and property-based testing with StreamData.

### Topic Notes

- ExUnit Basics, test modules, assertions, and test helpers
- Fixtures and Setup, ExUnit.Case, setup blocks, and shared fixtures
- Mocking and Stubs, Mox and behaviour-based mocking
- [Property-Based Testing](https://alevel.wyattau.com/computer-science/software-engineering/02-testing/), StreamData and generative testing

### Key Concepts

**ExUnit** uses the `test` macro and `assert`/`refute` for assertions. Tests are organized in modules with `use ExUnit.Case`. The `describe` block groups related tests. Tests can run asynchronously with `async: true`.

**Mox** is the standard mocking library. It defines behaviours that test doubles implement. Mox ensures test isolation by verifying that mocks are defined before tests run. It avoids the pitfalls of traditional mocking.

**Fixtures** provide test data. ExUnit supports setup blocks that create fixtures and inject them into tests. The `let` pattern from other frameworks is replaced by `setup` blocks and module attributes.

---

## Learning Path

Elixir's learning curve is moderate. The functional paradigm is approachable, and OTP provides structure. Follow this progression.

### Stage 1: Elixir Foundations (Weeks 1–3)

- Learn variables, pattern matching, and functions
- Understand modules, attributes, and documentation
- Write small programs using recursion and Enum

### Stage 2: Processes and OTP (Weeks 4–7)

- Learn process basics, spawn, send, receive
- Master GenServer and the supervision tree
- Study OTP Application and fault tolerance

### Stage 3: Phoenix (Weeks 8–12)

- Build web applications with Phoenix router and controllers
- Learn Ecto for database access and changesets
- Study Channels and LiveView for real-time features

### Stage 4: Advanced (Weeks 13–16)

- Study distributed Elixir and clustering
- Learn testing with Mox and property-based testing
- Build a production-ready application with supervision trees

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I learn Elixir or Ruby first?

If your goal is web development, learn Ruby first, it is more widely used and has a larger ecosystem. If your goal is concurrent, fault-tolerant systems, learn Elixir, its process model and OTP are unmatched. Elixir's syntax is Ruby-inspired, so learning Ruby first makes Elixir easier.

### What is the difference between Elixir and Erlang?

Elixir runs on the Erlang VM (BEAM) and can use any Erlang library. Elixir provides a more modern syntax, better tooling (Mix, Hex), and a more productive developer experience. Erlang is more established in telecom and mission-critical systems. Choose Elixir for new projects.

### What is "let it crash"?

"Let it crash" is the OTP philosophy of fault tolerance. Instead of defensively checking for every possible error, you write code that handles the happy path and lets unexpected errors crash the process. A supervisor detects the crash and restarts the process with a clean state. This makes systems self-healing.

### Is Elixir good for CPU-bound work?

The BEAM VM is optimized for I/O-bound and concurrent work, not CPU-bound computation. If you need heavy computation, use a NIF (Native Implemented Function) in C or Rust, or delegate to a specialized service. Elixir excels at handling many concurrent connections, not heavy computation.

### What is LiveView and when should I use it?

LiveView renders HTML on the server and pushes updates over WebSocket. It eliminates the need for a JavaScript framework for most real-time features. Use LiveView for dashboards, real-time feeds, and interactive forms. For complex client-side interactions, you may still need JavaScript.

### How do I deploy a Phoenix application?

Use Mix releases for deployment. `mix release` builds a self-contained release with the Erlang VM. Deploy to servers, containers (Docker), or platforms like Gigalixir, Fly.io, and Render. For production, configure Ecto, error tracking (Sentry), and monitoring.

## Index

sources:
  - text: Standard textbook reference



import { Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Elixir is a programming language with a rich type system and ecosystem. Work through the Elixir sections in order, starting with Advanced and Basics and building toward Advanced, Basics, Concurrency, Functions Modules and Intro, then check yourself with the practice problems for each topic.

## Intuition

Elixir is like a team of skilled workers, each with their own workspace and tools. They communicate by passing notes rather than sharing a whiteboard. This isolation means one worker's mistake does not corrupt another's work, and the supervisor can replace a worker without disrupting the team.

These notes guide you from the basics of the workshop (data types and pattern matching) to the advanced machinery (metaprogramming and OTP). Each section builds on the previous, like learning to use hand tools before power tools. Master the fundamentals, and the advanced topics become natural extensions of what you already know.

## Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Forgetting to use the pipe operator for function chaining

Elixir developers often nest function calls deeply, making code hard to read. The pipe operator `|>` passes the result of the left-hand expression as the first argument to the right-hand function. Instead of `Enum.sum(Enum.filter(Enum.map(list, &(&1 * 2)), &(&1 > 10)))`, write `list |> Enum.map(&(&1 * 2)) |> Enum.filter(&(&1 > 10)) |> Enum.sum()`. The pipe operator is idiomatic Elixir and makes data transformation pipelines clear.

### Mistake 2: Not using pattern matching for function clauses

Students often use conditional statements (`if`/`case`) inside a single function body instead of defining multiple function clauses with pattern matching. For example, instead of writing `def handle(:ok, data), do: ...` and `def handle(:error, reason), do: ...` as separate clauses, they write one function with a case statement. Multiple clauses are more readable and follow Elixir conventions.

### Mistake 3: Ignoring process isolation in concurrent code

Elixir processes are isolated by default -- they do not share memory. Students coming from shared-memory languages sometimes assume they can mutate shared state. Instead, use message passing (`send/2` and `receive`) or agents/ETS for shared state. Each process has its own heap and stack, so a crash in one process does not affect others unless you explicitly link them.

10 auto-graded practice problems covering core Elixir concepts. Select an answer, submit, and review

### Data Types and Pattern Matching

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What does `{a, b} = {1, 2}` do in Elixir?"} options={[ 'Binds a to 1 and b to 2', 'Checks if a equals 1 and b equals 2', 'Creates a tuple {1, 2} and assigns it to a', 'Raises a syntax error', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"The = operator is a match operator, not assignment. It matches the right side against the pattern on the left. Unbound variables (a, b) get bound to the corresponding values from the tuple."} difficulty="easy"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What is the result of `[0 | [1, 2, 3]]`?"} options={['[0, 1, 2, 3]', '[1, 2, 3, 0]', '{:ok, [0, 1, 2, 3]}', 'Syntax error']} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"The | operator prepends an element to a list. [0 | [1, 2, 3]]  produces [0, 1, 2, 3]. This is O(1) because it only creates a new head node pointing to the existing tail."} difficulty="easy"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What does `^x = 2` do if x is currently bound to 1?"} options={[ 'Raises a MatchError because x (1) does not equal 2', 'Rebinds x to 2', 'Returns false', 'Returns :error', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"The pin operator ^ prevents rebinding. ^x = 2 attempts to match x\'s current value (1) against 2. Since 1 != 2, it raises a MatchError. Without the pin, x = 2 would rebind x to 2."} difficulty="medium"  />

### Functions and Modules

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What is the difference between `def` and `defp` in a module?"} options={[ 'def is public, defp is private to the defining module', 'def is for functions, defp is for protocols', 'def compiles at runtime, defp compiles at compile time', 'def takes any number of args, defp takes exactly one', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"def defines a public function callable from any module. defp defines a private function only callable from within the defining module. Attempting to call a private function from outside raises UndefinedFunctionError."} difficulty="easy"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={'What does `&(&1 * 2)` create?'} options={[ 'An anonymous function that multiplies its argument by 2', 'A reference to a variable named &1', 'A macro that doubles values at compile time', 'A syntax error', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation="The & operator with positional arguments (&1, &2, etc.) creates an anonymous function shorthand. &(&1 *2) is equivalent to fn x -> x* 2 end. &1 is the first argument, &2 would be the second, and so on." difficulty="medium"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={`Which of the following correctly accesses the value associated with the key :name in the map \`%{name: "Alice", age: 30}\`?`} options={['map.name', 'map[:name] or map.name both work', 'map.get(:name)', 'map.fetch("name")']} correctAnswer={0} explanation="For maps with atom keys, the dot syntax (map.name) works and returns the value. map[:name]  also works and returns nil for missing keys. The dot syntax raises KeyError if the key is missing. map.get/2 is a Map module function, not a dot-access method." difficulty="easy"  />

### Concurrency and OTP

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What happens when a linked process crashes in Elixir?"} options={[ 'The linked process receives an exit signal and also crashes', 'Nothing happens because processes are isolated', 'The process is automatically restarted by the VM', 'A log message is written and the crash is ignored', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"spawn_link creates a bidirectional link. When one process exits abnormally, the exit signal propagates to the linked process, causing it to crash too. To prevent this, set Process.flag(:trap_exit, true) to receive {:EXIT, pid, reason} messages instead."} difficulty="medium"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"What is the difference between GenServer.call and GenServer.cast?"} options={[ 'call is synchronous (blocks for reply), cast is asynchronous (fire-and-forget)', 'call is for external callers, cast is for internal callers', 'call sends to a named process, cast sends to a PID', 'call uses TCP, cast uses UDP', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"GenServer.call/3 blocks the caller until handle_call/3 returns {:reply, reply, new_state}. GenServer.cast/2 returns :ok immediately and the server processes the message via handle_cast/2, returning {:noreply, new_state}."} difficulty="medium"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={"When should you use the `:one_for_all` supervision strategy?"} options={[ 'When children are tightly coupled and cannot function without each other', 'When each child is completely independent', 'When you want only the first child to restart', 'When children are on different machines', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation={"The :one_for_all strategy restarts ALL children when any single child crashes. This is appropriate for tightly coupled processes that share state or dependencies and cannot operate correctly if one component is missing."} difficulty="hard"  />

<PracticeProblem client:only="solid-js" question={'What does `quote do: 1 + 2` return in Elixir?'} options={[ 'An AST tuple: {:+, meta, [1, 2]}', 'The number 3', 'A string "1 + 2"', 'A macro definition', ]} correctAnswer={0} explanation="quote converts Elixir code into its Abstract Syntax Tree representation. 1 + 2 becomes {:+, [context: Elixir, imports: [{2, Kernel}]], [1, 2]} -- a three-element tuple with the operation atom, metadata, and argument list. Literals like integers represent themselves." difficulty="hard"  />

## Intuition

**Elixir brings functional programming to scalable systems:** Built on the Erlang VM, Elixir combines functional programming principles with tools for building fault-tolerant, distributed applications. Pattern matching and immutability are core to the language.

**Why it matters:** Elixir excels at real-time applications (chat, gaming, IoT) where thousands of concurrent connections must be handled efficiently.

**The key insight:** "Let it crash" is not sloppy coding, it is a deliberate strategy where supervised processes restart in known good states, creating systems that are more reliable than those that try to handle every error manually.

## Phoenix Practice

5 exercises covering LiveView patterns, PubSub broadcasting, context modules, changeset validation, and channel communication.

---

### Exercise 1: LiveView Patterns

**Problem:** Build a real-time counter with LiveView that displays the current value and supports increment, decrement, and reset. Include a `mount/3` callback and proper event handling with `handle_event/3`.

```elixir
defmodule MyAppWeb.CounterLive do
  use MyAppWeb, :live_view

  @impl true
  def mount(_params, _session, socket) do
    \{:ok, assign(socket, count: 0)\}
  end

  @impl true
  def render(assigns) do
    ~H"""
    <div class="counter-container">
      <h1>Counter: <%= @count %></h1>

      <div class="buttons">
        <button phx-click="decrement" class="btn btn-secondary">-</button>
        <button phx-click="reset" class="btn btn-outline">Reset</button>
        <button phx-click="increment" class="btn btn-primary">+</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    """
  end

  @impl true
  def handle_event("increment", _params, socket) do
    \{:noreply, assign(socket, count: socket.assigns.count + 1)\}
  end

  def handle_event("decrement", _params, socket) do
    \{:noreply, assign(socket, count: socket.assigns.count - 1)\}
  end

  def handle_event("reset", _params, socket) do
    \{:noreply, assign(socket, count: 0)\}
  end
end
```

**Solution:** `mount/3` initializes the socket with `count: 0`. `render/1` returns HEEx template with `phx-click` bindings. Each `handle_event/3` clause pattern matches the event name and updates `socket.assigns`. The `~H` sigil enables compile-time template validation. `{:noreply, socket}` prevents sending a message back to the client.

---

### Exercise 2: PubSub Broadcasting

**Problem:** Implement a LiveView that subscribes to a PubSub topic and updates in real time when a broadcast occurs. Include a form that broadcasts new messages to all connected clients.

```elixir
defmodule MyAppWeb.ChatLive do
  use MyAppWeb, :live_view

  @topic "chat_room"

  @impl true
  def mount(_params, _session, socket) do
    if connected?(socket) do
      Phoenix.PubSub.subscribe(MyApp.PubSub, @topic)
    end

    \{:ok,
     socket
     |> assign(messages: [], new_message: "")\}
  end

  @impl true
  def render(assigns) do
    ~H"""
    <div class="chat-container">
      <h2>Chat Room</h2>

      <div class="messages" id="messages">
        <div :for={msg <- @messages} class="message">
          <strong><%= msg.user %>:</strong> <%= msg.text %>
          <small><%= msg.timestamp %></small>
        </div>
      </div>

      <form phx-submit="send_message">
        <input
          type="text"
          name="message"
          value={@new_message}
          placeholder="Type a message..."
          autocomplete="off"
        />
        <button type="submit">Send</button>
      </form>
    </div>
    """
  end

  @impl true
  def handle_event("send_message", %\{"message" => text\}, socket) do
    message = %\{
      user: socket.assigns.current_user.name,
      text: text,
      timestamp: NaiveDateTime.utc_now()
    \}

    Phoenix.PubSub.broadcast(MyApp.PubSub, @topic, \{:new_message, message\})

    \{:noreply, assign(socket, new_message: "")\}
  end

  @impl true
  def handle_info(\{:new_message, message\}, socket) do
    messages = socket.assigns.messages ++ [message]
    \{:noreply, assign(socket, messages: Enum.take(messages, -50))\}
  end
end
```

**Solution:** `connected?(socket)` checks if the LiveView is connected (not SSR). `PubSub.subscribe` listens to the topic. `PubSub.broadcast` sends to all subscribers. `handle_info/2` receives the broadcast and updates the socket. `Enum.take(messages, -50)` keeps only the last 50 messages to prevent unbounded growth.

---

### Exercise 3: Context Module

**Problem:** Implement a context module for a blog that provides a clean API for articles, including listing, creating, updating, and publishing. The context should hide the underlying schema details.

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Blog do
  import Ecto.Query

  alias MyApp.Repo
  alias MyApp.Blog.Article

  def list_published_articles do
    Article
    |> Article.published()
    |> Article.order_by_newest()
    |> Repo.all()
  end

  def get_article!(id), do: Repo.get!(Article, id)

  def get_article_by_slug!(slug) do
    Repo.get_by!(Article, slug: slug)
  end

  def create_article(attrs \\ %\{\}) do
    %Article\{\}
    |> Article.changeset(attrs)
    |> Repo.insert()
  end

  def update_article(%Article\{\} = article, attrs) do
    article
    |> Article.changeset(attrs)
    |> Repo.update()
  end

  def publish_article(%Article\{\} = article) do
    article
    |> Article.publish_changeset()
    |> Repo.update()
  end

  def delete_article(%Article\{\} = article) do
    Repo.delete(article)
  end

  def change_article(%Article\{\} = article, attrs \\ %\{\}) do
    Article.changeset(article, attrs)
  end
end

defmodule MyApp.Blog.Article do
  use Ecto.Schema
  import Ecto.Changeset

  schema "articles" do
    field :title, :string
    field :body, :string
    field :slug, :string
    field :status, :string, default: "draft"
    field :published_at, :naive_datetime
    belongs_to :user, MyApp.Accounts.User

    timestamps()
  end

  def changeset(article, attrs) do
    article
    |> cast(attrs, [:title, :body, :slug])
    |> validate_required([:title, :body, :slug])
    |> validate_length(:title, max: 200)
    |> unique_constraint(:slug)
  end

  def publish_changeset(article) do
    article
    |> change(status: "published", published_at: NaiveDateTime.utc_now())
    |> validate_required([:title, :body])
  end

  def published do
    from a in __MODULE__,
      where: a.status == "published" and not is_nil(a.published_at)
  end

  def order_by_newest(query \\ __MODULE__) do
    from a in query,
      order_by: [desc: a.published_at]
  end
end
```

**Solution:** The context module `Blog` provides the public API. All queries go through `Repo`. Schema functions (`published/0`, `order_by_newest/1`) compose in queries. `change_article/2` returns a changeset for form prefilling. The schema separates data concerns from business logic. The context is efficiently mockable in tests.

---

### Exercise 4: Changeset Validation

**Problem:** Build a registration form changeset with complex validations: password confirmation, terms acceptance, email format, and username constraints. Include custom validators.

```elixir
defmodule MyApp.Accounts.User do
  use Ecto.Schema
  import Ecto.Changeset

  schema "users" do
    field :email, :string
    field :username, :string
    field :password, :string, virtual: true, redact: true
    field :password_confirmation, :string, virtual: true, redact: true
    field :hashed_password, :string, redact: true
    field :terms_accepted, :boolean, default: false
    field :display_name, :string
    timestamps()
  end

  def registration_changeset(user, attrs) do
    user
    |> cast(attrs, [:email, :username, :password, :password_confirmation, :terms_accepted, :display_name])
    |> validate_required([:email, :username, :password, :password_confirmation, :terms_accepted])
    |> validate_format(:email, ~r/^[^\s]+@[^\s]+$/, message: "must be a valid email address")
    |> validate_length(:username, min: 3, max: 30)
    |> validate_format(:username, ~r/^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$/, message: "can only contain letters, numbers, and underscores")
    |> validate_length(:password, min: 8, max: 100)
    |> validate_confirmation(:password)
    |> validate_acceptance(:terms_accepted, message: "must be accepted to create an account")
    |> validate_terms()
    |> validate_display_name()
    |> unique_constraint(:email)
    |> unique_constraint(:username)
    |> hash_password()
  end

  defp validate_terms(changeset) do
    if get_change(changeset, :terms_accepted) == true do
      changeset
    else
      add_error(changeset, :terms_accepted, "must be accepted")
    end
  end

  defp validate_display_name(changeset) do
    case get_change(changeset, :display_name) do
      nil ->
        changeset

      name when byte_size(name) < 2 ->
        add_error(changeset, :display_name, "must be at least 2 characters")

      name ->
        if String.contains?(name, ~w(admin root superuser)) do
          add_error(changeset, :display_name, "contains a reserved word")
        else
          changeset
        end
    end
  end

  defp hash_password(changeset) do
    case get_change(changeset, :password) do
      nil -> changeset
      password ->
        change(changeset, hashed_password: Bcrypt.hash_pwd_salt(password))
    end
  end
end
```

**Solution:** Virtual fields (`:password`, `:password_confirmation`) are not persisted. `validate_confirmation` checks password match. `validate_acceptance` requires terms acceptance. Custom validators (`validate_terms`, `validate_display_name`) add business-specific rules. `hash_password` is called only when the password changes. `redact: true` prevents sensitive fields from appearing in logs.

---

### Exercise 5: Channel Communication

**Problem:** Implement a Phoenix Channel for real-time presence tracking. The channel should handle user joins, track online users, broadcast presence updates, and handle disconnections.

```elixir
defmodule MyAppWeb.PresenceChannel do
  use Phoenix.Channel

  alias MyApp.Presence

  @impl true
  def join("presence:lobby", %\{"user_id" => user_id\}, socket) do
    send(self(), :after_join)
    \{:ok, assign(socket, user_id: user_id)\}
  end

  def join(_topic, _params, _socket) do
    \{:error, %\{reason: "unauthorized"\}\}
  end

  @impl true
  def handle_info(:after_join, socket) do
    \{:ok, _\} =
      Presence.track(socket, socket.assigns.user_id, %\{
        joined_at: System.system_time(:second),
        username: get_username(socket.assigns.user_id)
      \})

    push(socket, "presence_state", Presence.list(socket))
    \{:noreply, socket\}
  end

  @impl true
  def handle_in("message:new", %\{"text" => text\}, socket) do
    broadcast!(socket, "message:new", %\{
      user_id: socket.assigns.user_id,
      text: text,
      timestamp: System.system_time(:second)
    \})

    \{:reply, :ok, socket\}
  end

  def handle_in("typing", %\{"typing" => typing\}, socket) do
    broadcast_from!(socket, "typing", %\{
      user_id: socket.assigns.user_id,
      typing: typing
    \})

    \{:noreply, socket\}
  end

  def handle_in("message:react", %\{"message_id" => msg_id, "emoji" => emoji\}, socket) do
    broadcast!(socket, "message:reacted", %\{
      message_id: msg_id,
      user_id: socket.assigns.user_id,
      emoji: emoji
    \})

    \{:noreply, socket\}
  end

  defp get_username(user_id) do
    case MyApp.Accounts.get_user(user_id) do
      nil -> "Unknown"
      user -> user.username
    end
  end
end

defmodule MyApp.Presence do
  use Phoenix.Presence,
    otp_app: :my_app,
    pubsub_server: MyApp.PubSub
end
```

**Solution:** `join/3` authenticates and stores the user ID in the socket. `Presence.track` registers the user with metadata. `handle_info(:after_join)` runs after join completes. `broadcast!` sends to all subscribers. `broadcast_from!` sends to all except the sender (used for typing indicators). `Presence.list` returns all tracked presences. The Presence module is configured via `use Phoenix.Presence`.

## Intuition

**Phoenix is Elixir's web framework, optimised for real-time:** Phoenix uses channels and LiveView to build interactive web applications without writing JavaScript. The BEAM VM's concurrency model handles thousands of simultaneous connections efficiently.

**Why it matters:** Phoenix enables building real-time features (live dashboards, collaborative editing, chat) that are difficult to achieve with traditional request-response frameworks.

**The key insight:** LiveView renders HTML on the server and sends only diffs to the client, this eliminates the complexity of client-side state management while delivering a responsive user experience.

## Common Mistakes

**Confusing processes with OS threads:** Elixir/Erlang processes are lightweight (a few KB) and scheduled by the BEAM VM, not the OS. You can spawn millions of processes. Do not worry about thread pools or OS-level concurrency limits.

**Blocking in GenServer handle_info:** `handle_info` callbacks run in the GenServer process. If you perform blocking I/O (HTTP calls, file reads), the entire GenServer blocks. Use Task.async or spawn separate processes for blocking work.

**Ignoring OTP supervision tree design:** Supervisors restart failed processes. If your supervision strategy is `:one_for_one` but processes depend on each other, restarting one may leave others in an inconsistent state. Design supervision trees to match your applications dependency structure.
